..
Issued at 250 PM EDT Wed Aug 19 2026

Rest of Today-Tonight...Despite soundings and GOES imagery 
showing PWATs at or above 2.0" (well above the 90th percentile for
the time of year), inhibition has out over North and East Central
Florida this morning/most of this afternoon (apparent by the 
anemic cu-field), and thunderstorms had been confined to West 
Central Florid until now. Showers and storms have finally begun to
pop over our area, but continue to struggle. The latest HRRR runs
have been doing decent job capturing the evolution so far, albeit
with lower coverage than reality, and the official forecast has 
been adjusted closer to those solutions. Rain and storm chances 
remain near to slightly above normal, but the highest chances
(around 60%) are now confined to the southern counties in the 
evening where outflow from the current activity is forecast to 
collide with the slowed east coast sea breeze. That said, the rest
of the area sports a broad 40-50% chance. Storms that manage to 
develop could become strong and produce gusty winds 45-55 mph, 
frequent cloud to ground lightning, and a quick 1-3" of rainfall 
leading to localized flooding. It's hot with all the sunshine. 
Temperatures have reached the L-M90s, and a few spots have hit 
the U90s, with a little more daytime heating still to go. A 
couple record high temperatures could be hit before the end of the
day. Peak afternoon heat indices up to around 112 are expected, 
and a Heat Advisory remains in effect until 8 PM. 

Thursday-Friday...Little change at the surface. Offshore (SW-S)
flow across the peninsula will continue between a quasi-
stationary front draped across the southeast and high pressure 
over the Atlantic. Aloft, a mid-level disturbance is forecast to 
develop over Florida at the base of the trough stationed over the 
eastern US. Between lingering high moisture (PWATs generally 
1.8-2.0"), the upper level support, and offshore flow favoring a 
sea breeze collision on the eastern side of the peninsula, rain 
chances remain above normal (45-65%), though some drier air (PWATs
down to 1.7") may sneak into low-mid levels and result in chances
lower than currently advertised. Some modest cooling in the mid-
levels could support wider coverage stronger storms capable of 
wind gusts 45-55 mph, and a few locally damaging gusts around 60 
mph can't be ruled out. Frequent to excessive cloud to ground 
lightning, and locally heavy rainfall leading to minor flooding 
are also possible. There is also a very low chance for a funnel 
cloud to develop given all the boundary collisions. Heat will 
remain a concern. Although increased cloud cover and rain chances 
shave a degree or two off temperatures, bringing highs closer to 
normal in the L-M90s, the high humidity will keep peak afternoon 
heat indices in the U100s-L110s Thursday, and the M-U100s Friday.
Yet more Heat Advisories may be needed. Residents and visitors 
should continue to practice heat safety, and avoid extended 
exposure or take frequent breaks during the hottest part of the 
day.

Saturday-Tuesday...A little bit of uncertainty in the extended
forecast, but generally expect the hot and stormy afternoons to
continue. The surface pattern remains largely unchanged, with the
quasi-stationary front continuing its residency over the
Southeast, keeping the Bermuda high ridge axis shunted south of 
Central Florida, and us in offshore (SW-S) flow favoring a sea 
breeze collision over the eastern half of the peninsula. The 
upper-level pattern over the CONUS amplifies as energy dives into 
the trough over the eastern US, though models disagree whether 
this energy will remain more a shortwave or develop into a mid- 
level low. A shortwave would cause less amplification and keep 
impulses of energy transiting the pattern more north of Florida, 
while a mid-level low would cause the trough to dig farther 
south, allowing more of the energy to reach the Florida. Worth 
noting there's also been some model disagreement over how strong 
these impulses will be, with some solutions developing a another 
mid-level low. All this to say, could see above normal rain 
chances late this weekend, depending where and how the upper level
energy that could enhance convection evolves. For now, official 
forecast calls for slightly above normal rain chances through the 
weekend. The trough retreats north the first half of next week, 
but additional impulses of energy will continue to swing by in the
flow aloft, supporting near normal rain chances despite some 
drier air intruding at times, which may result rain chances 
decreases for some spots in future forecast as confidence 
increases. Temperatures remain slightly above normal with highs in
the L-M90s, which combined with the humidity result in peak 
afternoon heat indices to around 107, just shy of Heat Advisory.
